findings.where: Screen 7 'Its equation' text (and explain paragraph 7, and the picture's first working row)
findings.what: It opens 'Multiply it out', but 'it' points back two screens to n · (r − p) = 0, past a puzzle. It also skips the key step to 2(x − 1) + 1(y − 1) + 2(z − 3) = 0: write r = (x, y, z), so r − p = (x − 1, y − 1, z − 3), then dot it with (2, 1, 2). Lead with the point ('A plane's equation has the normal's parts in front of x, y and z'), then show that line.

findings.where: Screen 7 readout tiles at 360 px during the demonstration (film sheet s6, rows 2-3)
findings.what: As r glides to the origin, the r − p tile's value '(−0.8, −0.9, −2.8)' runs past the tile's right edge, and '(0.6, −0.2, −1.4)' fills it edge to edge. Show whole numbers while moving, or let a long value take the whole row.

'The laser also cannot tell you which side a point is on, or how far away it is' is not true of a rotating laser used with its receiver. The receiver's up and down arrows, and on many a millimetre offset, give exactly the side and the distance. Say the beam alone cannot, and that the receiver's arrows are the sign of n · (r − p).

One screen holds two ideas, the equation and the distance from a point to the plane. It never says why the part of the step along n is the distance: moving within the plane leaves the reading unchanged, so the straight-on route is along n.

It puts the line into the equation without first writing its point as (t, 1 + 2t, 0), as puzzle 12's why does with (1, t, t). 'The reading' has nothing to anchor it in a read-through, so name it n · (r − p).

findings.where: Screen 1 picture (360 light opening) and screen 2
findings.what: The first line lies flat in the floor (z = 0), and the low view turns the scene into a thin strip with about 170 px of blank above it. Nothing looks like 'space' until screen 3. Give screen 1 a line with a z part, or raise the view.

findings.where: Screen 1 picture labels at the start point (360 px)
findings.what: 't = 0', 'p', the z-axis tick and 'r' crowd within about 40 px of the start point. They are legible but cluttered. Offset 't = 0' from the z axis, or hide 'r' while the dot sits on p.

findings.where: Screens 4 and 6 readouts mid-motion (film sheets s4, s6)
findings.what: Each tile is rounded on its own, so one frame shows r − p = (0.6, −0.2, −1.4) beside n · (r − p) = −1.6. Worked by hand, those numbers give −1.8. Work the reading from the rounded step, or round only at whole steps.
'Every mix s u + t w fills a plane through the origin' is not quite right, because each mix is one point. It should read 'All the mixes s u + t w fill a plane through the origin'.

findings.where: Screen 5 'A plane and its normal' text
findings.what: 'Stands square to it' is never unpacked on screen; the explain's 'at right angles to every line in the plane' would help. The screen also states the reading is 0 without the short working 2 + 0 − 2 = 0.

findings.where: The right-angle mark at p on the normal (screens 5-8 and 13, at 360 and 1280)
findings.what: It draws as a tiny smudge beside p ('p :'), too small to read as a square corner. Enlarge it or drop it.
In 'The 9 is n · p. So (2, 1, 2) is on the plane, as 4 + 1 + 4 = 9.', the 'So' does not follow from the sentence before. Start it as a check: 'Check a point. (2, 1, 2) gives 4 + 1 + 4 = 9.'

findings.where: Practice worked example (plane through three points)
findings.what: The cross product is written with × as plain multiplication, as in '(2 × 3 − 0 × 0, …)', right after u × w meant the cross product. Write the parts as 6 − 0, 0 + 3, 0 + 2 instead.

findings.where: Lesson as a whole versus the brief
findings.what: Two planes meeting along the cross of their normals, and the plane through three points, are in the brief. They appear only in the notes (explain, practice), with no screen or puzzle. One mixed puzzle on either would let Dan try them.
